description: Believers and non-believers in Surah al-Baqarah, the Qur'anic creation account, and humanity as khalifah.
content_html:
Believers and Non-Believers in Surah al-Baqarah

Surah al-Baqarah (Surah 2) is the longest chapter in the Qur’an and one of the most important. Its name, meaning “the Cow,” refers to the story of Moses and a miraculous cow in verses 67–73. The surah opens with a description of three groups of people, presenting a moral map of humanity from the Qur’an’s perspective.

Those who believe are described as people who believe in the unseen, establish prayer, give from what Allah has provided, believe in what was revealed to Muhammad and in earlier revelations, and are certain of the hereafter. For them, the Qur’an says, “such are on guidance from their Lord and such are the successful.” Their faith is active: it manifests in prayer, generosity and moral seriousness, not merely in intellectual assent.

Those who disbelieve are described as people for whom warning makes no difference — their hearts are sealed, their hearing and sight are covered. This language uses the Qur’anic concept of the “sealed heart” — not a physical sealing but a description of a state of moral hardening caused by repeated rejection of truth. A third group, the hypocrites, claim to believe but do not. The Qur’an treats hypocrisy as more dangerous than open disbelief, because it corrupts the community from within.

Key Fact

In Surah al-Baqarah, the believer is someone who: (1) believes in the unseen, (2) establishes prayer, (3) gives from what Allah has provided. Their faith is not passive — it is expressed through worship, generosity and moral action. This portrait of the believer shapes Islamic practice: faith and action cannot be separated.

The Qur’anic Account of Creation

The Qur’an does not give a single unified creation narrative like Genesis 1–2. Instead, creation references are spread across many surahs, each emphasising a different aspect. Several key verses are specified. In Surah 21:30, Allah declares: “Do not the unbelievers see that the heavens and the earth were joined together (as one unit of creation), before We clove them asunder?” This verse is often cited in discussions of whether the Qur’an anticipates modern scientific theories about the origins of the universe. Muslim scholars debate the significance of this verse in relation to cosmology.

Surah 41:11 describes Allah addressing the heavens while they were “smoke” and commanding them and the earth to come into existence willingly or unwillingly — they replied: “We come, in willing obedience.” This passage emphasises that creation is an act of divine command (the Qur’anic concept of Kun fa-yakun — “Be! And it is”). Surah 7:54 states that Allah created the heavens and earth in six “days” (the Arabic word ayyam can mean periods or eras rather than 24-hour days) and then “established himself on the Throne”.

In Surah 45:3–5, creation itself is presented as a sign (ayah) of Allah’s existence and power: the alternation of night and day, the provision of rain, the diversity of languages and colours — all are described as signs “for people of understanding.” This approach — reading the natural world as a testimony to Allah — is a central feature of Qur’anic theology. The universe is not an accident but a deliberate act of communication from the Creator.

Humanity as Khalifah: Surah 2:30–39

One of the most important theological concepts in the Qur’an about human beings is the idea of khalifah. In Surah 2:30–39, Allah announces to the angels: “I will create a vicegerent on earth.” The word khalifah means successor, steward or vicegerent — someone who acts on behalf of another. The angels protest: “Will you place therein one who will spread corruption and shed blood while we glorify your praise?” Allah replies: “I know what you do not know.”

Adam is then created and taught the names of all things — a privilege not given to the angels. When Adam demonstrates this knowledge, Allah commands the angels to bow to Adam. They all do, except Iblis, who refuses out of pride. Iblis becomes the tempter of humanity. Adam and his wife are placed in the garden but warned not to eat from one tree; Iblis deceives them, they eat, and they are sent to live on earth. Allah, however, forgives Adam when he repents — showing that human beings are created weak but capable of repentance and restoration.

The concept of khalifah has profound ethical implications. If humanity is Allah’s steward on earth, then human beings are accountable for how they treat the environment, other creatures and other people. They are trustees, not owners. This forms the Qur’anic basis for environmental ethics in Islam — the earth belongs to Allah, and humans must care for it accordingly.

Both the Qur’an and the Bible present creation as the deliberate act of one God, who creates humanity with a special status above other creatures. Both have a story of a garden, a temptation, a fall and expulsion. Both use six “days” or periods of creation.

Key differences: In the Qur’anic account, Adam repents and is forgiven — there is no concept of “original sin” passed to all humanity. In Islamic theology, human beings are born in a state of fitrah (natural purity) rather than sinfulness. The Qur’an does not name Adam’s wife in these passages. Responsibility for the disobedience is shared more equally between Adam and his wife in the Qur’an than in some readings of Genesis 3, where the woman is often held more responsible.

Modern Muslim scholars and activists draw on the concept of khalifah to argue for Islamic environmental ethics. If humanity is entrusted with the earth as Allah’s steward, then environmental destruction is a form of betrayal of that trust — a spiritual as well as an ethical failure. The Islamic Foundation for Ecology and Environmental Sciences (IFEES) has developed this theology in practical work on conservation.

The concept of khalifah also extends to social justice: as stewards, humans are accountable for how they treat the poor, the marginalised and the oppressed. The same Surah 2 that establishes the believer’s identity also contains laws on just economic dealings, care for orphans and widows, and the payment of zakah (almsgiving). Stewardship is both environmental and social.

Key Fact

Khalifah means vicegerent, steward or successor. In Surah 2:30–39, Allah appoints humanity as his khalifah on earth. This means human beings are trustees, not owners, of the natural world — accountable to Allah for how they treat creation. This is the Qur’anic basis for Islamic environmental ethics and social justice.
exam_tip_html: For “Explain two with sources” questions on creation or khalifah, cite the surah reference: “In Surah 2:30, Allah announces ‘I will create a vicegerent on earth’…” gives you the source mark. For 12-mark Discuss questions, the angles question (non-religious view) might challenge whether the creation account is scientific or simply mythological — develop the Muslim response fully, including how Qur’anic creation is read as sign rather than scientific textbook. Remember to distinguish Surah al-Baqarah (Surah 2) from other surahs — it is the longest surah and contains many different topics. SPaG: spell ‘khalifah’ (or ‘vicegerent’) and ‘Bismillah’ correctly; use ‘Iblis’ (not ‘Shaytan’) when referring to Surah 2’s account.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Surah al-Baqarah (Surah 2) describes the true believer as active in faith — praying, giving, trusting Allah — while non-believers have ‘sealed hearts’ and hypocrites are considered more dangerous than open unbelief.
  • The Qur’an presents creation across multiple surahs (45:3–5; 21:30; 41:11; 7:54): creation is an act of divine command (Kun fa-yakun) and the natural world is a sign (ayah) pointing to Allah’s existence.
  • Humanity as khalifah (steward/vicegerent — Surah 2:30–39) means humans are trustees of the earth accountable to Allah, forming the Qur’anic basis for Islamic environmental ethics and social responsibility.

practice_questions.text: Outline three characteristics of the believer as described in Surah al-Baqarah.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per discrete point:
• Believers believe in the unseen — they trust in Allah, angels, and the hereafter without direct sensory proof.
• They establish regular prayer (salah) — their faith is expressed through structured, daily acts of worship.
• They give from what Allah has provided — their belief is shown in generosity and care for others.

practice_questions.text: Describe the story of Adam as khalifah in Surah 2:30-39.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per point:
• Allah announced to the angels that he would create a vicegerent (khalifah) on earth; the angels questioned this because humans would cause corruption.
• Adam was taught the names of all things and the angels were commanded to bow to him — all did except Iblis, who refused.
• Adam and his wife were placed in a garden, tempted by Iblis, and sent to earth when they disobeyed; Allah forgave Adam when he repented.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the Qur'anic creation account shows what Allah is like.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks per point:
• Creation demonstrates Allah's absolute power — the concept of Kun fa-yakun ('Be! And it is') in passages like Surah 41:11 shows that Allah creates simply by speaking; nothing can resist or limit his creative command.
• Creation is a sign pointing to Allah — Surah 45:3-5 describes the alternation of night and day, the provision of rain and the diversity of creation as signs for 'people of understanding'; Allah communicates his existence through the natural world.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two ways in which the concept of khalifah affects how Muslims live today.
In your answer, refer to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks per point plus one for named source:
• Khalifah means Muslims see themselves as stewards of the earth, not its owners — they are accountable to Allah for how they treat the environment, giving Islamic support for conservation and opposition to wasteful consumption.
• Khalifah also extends to social justice: as stewards, Muslims are responsible for the fair distribution of wealth and care for the vulnerable — this connects to the payment of zakah and the commitment to justice found throughout Surah 2.
The fifth mark requires citing Surah 2:30 (or the khalifah passage) as the named source.

practice_questions.text:
'The Qur'anic teaching that humans are khalifah is the most important teaching about human beings in Islam.'
Discuss this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12): Both sides developed with named sources; justified conclusion.
Secure (7-9): Both sides present; at least one source.
Developing (4-6): One side stronger; few sources.
Emerging (1-3): Minimal.

In support: Khalifah establishes humanity's unique relationship with Allah — above the angels (who bowed to Adam), trusted with the earth, accountable at Judgement. It underpins both environmental ethics and social justice in Islam. The passage (Surah 2:30-39) is foundational for understanding human dignity and responsibility.
Against: Some would argue the doctrine of Tawhid is more fundamental — without understanding who Allah is, the concept of human stewardship has no context. Others might argue the Five Pillars are the most important expression of what it means to be human in Islam — they define the practical shape of Muslim life. Non-religious thinkers would question any teaching that grants humans a unique divine-given role, arguing that humans are simply one species among many with no special mandate.

practice_questions.text: Outline three ways in which Surah al-Baqarah describes non-believers and hypocrites.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per point:
• Non-believers are described as having 'sealed hearts' — they will not respond to warning because they have hardened themselves against truth.
• Their hearing and sight are described as covered — they cannot receive the message of the Qur'an.
• Hypocrites claim to believe but do not — the Qur'an treats them as more dangerous than open unbelievers because they corrupt the community from within.

knowledge_checks.q: What does the word 'khalifah' mean in Surah 2:30?
In Surah 2:30-39, which being refused to bow to Adam when commanded by Allah?
Surah 21:30 states that the heavens and earth were once _____ together before Allah separated them.
The Surah 2 description of believers says they 'establish _____ and give from what Allah has provided.'
Match each creation surah to its main teaching:
right: The heavens and earth were once joined, then separated
Creation is a sign for people of understanding
Humanity as khalifah — Allah's steward on earth

flashcard_questions.q: What does khalifah mean in Islamic theology?
flashcard_questions.a: Vicegerent, steward or successor — humanity as Allah's representative on earth.

flashcard_questions.q: Which surah establishes humanity as khalifah?
What did the angels say when Allah announced he would create a khalifah?
flashcard_questions.a: They questioned it — humans would cause corruption and shed blood.

flashcard_questions.q: What is Iblis in Islamic theology?
flashcard_questions.a: A jinn who refused to bow to Adam; became the tempter of humanity (equivalent to Satan).

flashcard_questions.q: What is Surah al-Baqarah and what does the name mean?
flashcard_questions.a: Surah 2 — the longest surah; 'The Cow', referring to a miracle of Moses in the text.

flashcard_questions.q: How does the Qur'an describe the believer in Surah 2?
flashcard_questions.a: Believes in the unseen, establishes prayer, gives generously from what Allah provides.
Allah's creative command: 'Be! And it is' — expressing his absolute power to create.

flashcard_questions.q: What does Surah 45:3-5 say about creation?
flashcard_questions.a: The natural world — night, day, rain, diversity — is a sign for people of understanding.

flashcard_questions.q: How does the Qur'an's account of the fall differ from the Bible's?
flashcard_questions.a: In the Qur'an, Adam repents and is forgiven — there is no concept of original sin passed to all humanity.

flashcard_questions.q: What Islamic term describes the state of natural purity in which humans are born?
flashcard_questions.a: Fitrah — the natural disposition towards Allah with which every human is born.

glossary_terms.definition: Surah 2 — the longest surah in the Qur'an, covering laws, beliefs and stories of earlier prophets; its name means 'The Cow'.
People described in the Qur'an as saying they believe but whose faith is insincere; also called hypocrites.
Surah 21, 'The Prophets'; verse 30 describes the heavens and earth as once joined together before Allah separated them.
The divine command 'Be!' by which Allah creates; from Arabic meaning 'to be', expressing Allah's absolute creative power.
Successor, steward or vicegerent; in Surah 2:30, Allah tells the angels he will place a khalifah on earth, understood as humanity acting as his steward and representative.
A jinn (spirit being) who refused to bow to Adam because of pride; the Islamic equivalent of Satan.
